sentences: In a soft, pale blue light, a woman in a summer kimono sits resting on a rock.
She holds a round fan in her hand, and behind her lie a calm lake and a line of mountains on the far shore.
This is Lakeside, painted in 1897 by the Japanese artist Kuroda Seiki on the shore of Lake Ashi in Hakone, a mountain area southwest of Tokyo.
It is an oil painting on canvas, and in 1999 it was designated an Important Cultural Property of Japan.
Kuroda was born in Kagoshima in 1866.
He went to France to study law, but chose painting instead and trained in Paris under Raphaël Collin.
He came home in 1893 and brought a bright new style of outdoor light to Japan.
In the summer of 1897, Kuroda went to Hakone to escape the heat.
His model was Kaneko Tane, later called Teruko, who would become his wife.
She remembered going to watch him work by the lake.
He asked her to sit on a rock, and she did.
From the next day he began to paint her and the view behind her.
With rainy and foggy days, it took about a month.
At that time, she said, he had been studying the water of the lake every day.
Now look at her clothes.
She wears a cotton summer kimono, pale blue with thin white stripes, and a dark blue sash.
The colour and pattern of the kimono echo the water behind her.
Look at the fan in her hand.
It is round and white, with small pink bush clover flowers, and she later said it came from the inn where they stayed.
She turns her head slightly to the left and gazes into the distance.
Now take in the colours of the whole picture.
Cool, pale blues hold everything together and capture the humid air of the highlands in summer.
The paint is thin, without the heavy shine of much oil painting.
Against all that blue, the small red notes of her lips and hairpin stand out.
A canvas of this size was normally used upright, for a figure.
Kuroda turned it on its side so that the lake and the mountains could share the space with her.
That autumn it was first shown at the White Horse Society, the group Kuroda had founded, under the title Summering.
In 1900 it went to the World's Fair in Paris.
In 1967 it appeared on a postage stamp, and it is now one of the best-loved Western-style paintings in Japan.
Kuroda died in 1924, and the painting was later given to the Kuroda Memorial Room in the hall built under his will.
Today it belongs to the Tokyo National Museum, as part of the Kuroda Memorial Hall collection in Ueno.
Step back and look at the whole scene.
By a lake in midsummer, a woman with a fan sits quietly and forgets the heat for a while.
Today, find one place where you can sit for a moment and feel a cool breeze.
